item.title: Talent diplomacy may become the next driver of global economic growth
item.description: As ageing populations and skill shortages weigh on economies worldwide, countries are looking beyond immigration to build structured talent partnerships. India has an opportunity to emerge as a trusted global hub for workforce readiness, backed by skills training, tech and verifiable credentials.
item.content:encoded:
The drivers of economic power have always traditionally been accessing to capital, energy, technology, and markets; but more nations are now running up against that much more difficult resource to generate fast talent.

Unlike capital, talent is not something that can be conjured out of thin air overnight, it takes years to educate, train, and ready the workforce. But at the same time that world economies are in need of more workers, the number of people available is declining.

Healthcare offers one of the most transparent indicators of this situation. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates a shortfall of 11. 1 million health and care professionals worldwide by 2030. Other sectors including manufacturing logistics hospitality, construction, and trades are experiencing similar pressures. Workforce numbers in many advanced countries are declining even as the need for core functions increases. There are declining numbers of people undertaking physically demanding jobs, leaving serious structural deficits difficult to address solely through large-scale migration.

What's left unsaid is huge: skills shortages are no longer an employment issue. They are a drag on economic growth. Countries are free to scale up investments in infrastructure, industrial capacity and technological advances, if they lack the people to run them, where is the growth?

Talent partnerships reshape economic diplomacy

Demographic decline is prompting governments to reconsider avenues for future growth. One-third of the EU population will be over 65 by the year 2050 and countries, including Japan and Germany, are already experiencing dire skill shortages within care and the healthcare sector.

Their answer has gone further than simply immigration reform. Germany's Skilled Immigration Act, Japan's increases of avenues for foreign workers and the EU's Talent Partnerships are part of a bigger change: policy makers are now starting to see "talent as a strategic asset".

These agreements are increasingly targeted on preparing the work force, recognising qualifications and moving workers, not only on visas. As countries used to compete for market access, energy, and supply chains, they are now forming partnerships to enjoy access to skilled people.

That may be one of the biggest changes to economic diplomacy in the coming decade.

India can become a global hub for workforce readiness

India’s opportunity should not be framed as the export of labour. It lies in becoming a trusted global centre for workforce readiness.

India’s domestic healthcare requirements must remain central to this approach. Responsible mobility should generate additional training capacity rather than draw indiscriminately from areas that already.

Encouragingly, this shift is already visible in policy. India plans to establish 30 Skill India International Centres focused on preparing individuals for overseas employment, while NSDC has certified over 22,455 candidates for international mobility over the past three years. The 2026 International Mobility Framework released by NITI Aayog further signals a shift in thinking, calling for greater state participation in global workforce mobility. Collectively, this suggests a larger shift where mobility of the workforce is a national asset helping create stronger economic partnerships, talent corridors, and help make India a trusted partner for the global workforce.

Technology must build trusted talent corridors

As opposed to taking over the role of educators, AI technology can assist in individualised learning, language training, workplace simulations, and competency evaluation.

Technology may minimise the information discrepancies, which have traditionally plagued international recruiting efforts. Employers require assurance that the credentials and experience are legitimate, while applicants require assurance about the legitimacy of the offer itself, along with its costs and conditions of employment.

This is increasingly becoming a competitive differentiator. ASEAN chases digital recognition of qualifications and credentials to enable smoother cross-border mobility.

For India, the opportunity is to make workforce readiness portable, verifiable and trusted. Technology can become the infrastructure that allows Indian professionals to prove their preparedness across markets, reducing friction for both employers and destination countries.

Though India's demographic weight is not the only one in an increasingly crowded field of developing countries, that invested years in creating structured talent corridors with host countries. Globally, over 8,000 nurses from Germany's Triple Win programme through government to government-built recruitment and training setups, while Japan's long standing health mobility corridors with Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam span language training, credentialing, and governance.

The real competition, therefore, is not for vacancies. It is for trust. Workforce shortages as a strategic challenge for ageing economies creates diplomacy where workforce readiness determines which nations become indispensable partners in supporting global growth.

(Mayank Kumar is the Co-founder & CEO of BorderPlus)

item.title: Workshaala targets Rs 1,000 Cr revenue as it scales enterprise workspace business
item.description:
Workshaala targets Rs 1,000 Cr revenue as it scales enterprise workspace business

item.content:encoded:
India's offices are being reinvented, and Workshaala wants to be the company that runs them. The enterprise workspace provider has set out a Rs 1,000 crore revenue vision for its next phase of growth, built on a footprint that already spans 3.5 million sq ft of serviceable area: 75,000 seats across 25 centres in 10 Indian cities.

The announcement follows a landmark moment for the company. Workshaala recently delivered what it describes as the world's largest service-platform workplace transaction, a deal that is now live within its existing footprint.

For the company's leadership, that transaction is less a finish line than a proof point. It shows the model works at the very top end of enterprise demand, and that it is ready to be replicated across the country.

From proof point to growth platform

Workshaala is clear that the Rs 1,000 crore target is not a fundraising story or a projection built on potential. It is a revenue roadmap anchored in a model the company has already tested at the largest scale in its category.

The timing reflects a market at an inflection point. India's technology and services economy is expected to add millions of white-collar seats over the next decade. Grade-A workspace demand is outpacing supply in every major city. And enterprises are taking a hard look at the economics of traditional real estate, seeking flexibility, cost predictability and operational efficiency without the weight of long-term leases.

That is precisely the gap Workshaala was built to fill. With execution already proven, the company sees scaling not as an option, but as the logical next step.

Four pillars to Rs 1,000 crore

Rather than a single bet on one city or one client segment, Workshaala's growth plan rests on four pillars, each already in motion.

1. Pan-India expansion. The company is growing across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and Mumbai, with emerging Tier II hubs such as Indore, Coimbatore and Chandigarh close behind. Enterprises increasingly want a single partner that can deliver consistent workspace standards in every city they operate in. Workshaala's playbook is designed to travel.

2. A technology layer beneath the real estate. Workshaala runs a platform that manages occupancy, utilization, service delivery and facility operations in real time. This lets it operate 75,000 seats across 25 centres with the discipline of a technology business rather than the margins of a facilities operator, and allows revenue to scale faster than headcount.

3. Enterprise-grade service delivery. Large corporates do not switch workspace partners lightly. They need assurance on uptime, compliance, safety, and consistency at scale. Workshaala's landmark transaction gives prospective clients a live reference they can visit before they sign, rather than a promise in a pitch deck.

4. Strategic ecosystem partnerships. Instead of competing with developers, landlords and corporate real estate teams, Workshaala works alongside them. It positions itself as the operating layer that makes large commercial assets enterprise-ready, a model that compounds as more partners plug into the platform.

Taken together, the pillars describe a company that is not chasing growth for its own sake, but extending a model it has already validated at scale.

Built for the GCC wave

No discussion of enterprise workspace demand in India is complete without Global Capability Centers, and this is where Workshaala sees its sharpest fit.

GCCs come with distinct expectations. Parent companies mandate strict security and compliance standards. Headcount plans can double within a year. And the space has to feel world-class from day one.

Workshaala's answer is to pair real estate execution with its live occupancy and service-delivery platform. Instead of waiting months for a customized build-out, a GCC can move into managed, technology-enabled space that is enterprise-ready from the outset. It can then grow from 200 seats to 2,000 without renegotiating its entire real estate strategy.

Standardized service levels across 25 centres in 10 cities mean every GCC location runs on the same playbook, with the uptime guarantees, compliance rigor, and reporting discipline a global headquarters expects.

As India cements its role as the world's hub for innovation and operations, GCCs are emerging as one of the fastest-growing segments of Workshaala's enterprise pipeline.

The road ahead

The next decade will decide how enterprise India works, and where. Companies want space that scales with them, runs reliably in every city and frees capital from long leases.

Workshaala is betting that the winners in this market will be operators who combine physical execution with a technology backbone, and that a model proven at the largest scale can be repeated city by city.

The Rs 1,000 crore milestone is the company's way of measuring that bet. With 75,000 seats already live, a reference transaction enterprises can walk into, and a growing GCC pipeline, Workshaala is entering its growth decade from a position of proof rather than promise.

item.title: Lessons in Chemistry: 5 Takeaways from Bonnie Garmus’ Novel
item.description: Discover five powerful lessons from Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus about equality, ambition, independent thinking, and self-worth.
item.content:encoded:
Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus is a thought-provoking novel about ambition, gender inequality, motherhood, and the courage to challenge social expectations.

Set in the 1960s, the story follows Elizabeth Zott, a brilliant chemist whose professional ambitions are constantly challenged by a society that believes women belong in the kitchen rather than the laboratory.

When Elizabeth unexpectedly becomes the host of a cooking television show, she uses the opportunity to teach more than recipes. Through science, she encourages women to think independently, question established beliefs, and recognise their own abilities.

The novel offers several meaningful lessons about self-worth, equality, and the importance of refusing to let society define who we can become.

5 Powerful ideas in Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus

1. Never let society define your potential

One of the most important lessons in Lessons in Chemistry is that your potential should never be determined by society's expectations.

Elizabeth Zott is an exceptionally talented scientist, but she faces discrimination because she is a woman working in a male-dominated field. Instead of being judged solely on her knowledge and abilities, she repeatedly encounters people who underestimate her because of her gender.

Her experiences highlight how social stereotypes can prevent talented individuals from reaching their full potential. Elizabeth refuses to accept these limitations as the truth about herself. She continues pursuing her interests and challenges the assumptions that attempt to hold her back.

The lesson is simple: your abilities are not limited by what others believe you can achieve. Whether in your career, education, or personal life, you deserve the opportunity to explore your potential without being restricted by outdated expectations.

2. Question everything instead of accepting it blindly

Elizabeth approaches life with the curiosity of a scientist. She believes in examining evidence, asking questions, and understanding why things happen rather than accepting conventional wisdom without thinking.

This mindset becomes particularly important when she begins hosting her cooking show, Supper at Six. Although the programme is designed around cooking, Elizabeth introduces scientific explanations and encourages her audience to understand the processes behind everyday tasks.

Her approach transforms an ordinary television show into an opportunity for women to learn, think critically, and develop confidence in their own intelligence.

The novel reminds readers that questioning established ideas is not necessarily an act of rebellion. Sometimes, it is the first step towards progress.

In everyday life, this means examining the beliefs we inherit, questioning unfair traditions, and making decisions based on reason rather than fear of judgement. Independent thinking allows us to recognise when something needs to change.

3. Women deserve equal opportunities and respect

Gender inequality is a central theme throughout Lessons in Chemistry. Elizabeth encounters professional discrimination, unequal treatment, and assumptions about what women should do with their lives.

Her experiences reflect a broader social problem: women's achievements have often been overlooked simply because they do not fit traditional expectations.

Through Elizabeth's journey, Bonnie Garmus illustrates how exhausting it can be to prove one's competence in an environment where others are unwilling to offer equal opportunities. Elizabeth must work harder to have her knowledge recognised, even when her qualifications speak for themselves.

However, the novel also demonstrates the importance of women supporting one another and recognising their shared potential.

The lesson extends beyond the workplace. Equality means respecting women's choices, valuing their contributions, and allowing them to pursue careers and ambitions without being forced into predefined roles.

A person's capabilities should determine their opportunities, not their gender.

7 Things to Accept About Yourself Before You Turn 30

4. Intelligence and confidence can change the way people think

Elizabeth's transformation into a television personality demonstrates that knowledge can be a powerful tool for challenging social attitudes.

Rather than abandoning her scientific background to fit the expectations of a cooking show, she brings science into the kitchen. She explains cooking through chemistry and treats her viewers as intelligent individuals capable of understanding complex ideas.

Her approach challenges the assumption that domestic responsibilities and intellectual pursuits must exist separately. It also gives women a platform to engage with science in a way that traditional institutions have often denied them.

Elizabeth's confidence is not about proving that she is better than everyone else. It comes from knowing the value of her knowledge and refusing to make herself smaller to satisfy other people's expectations.

This lesson encourages readers to embrace their expertise, communicate their ideas clearly, and trust their ability to make a difference.

Sometimes, changing people's perspectives begins with one person who is willing to challenge the familiar and present a different way of thinking.

5. Family and personal identity can exist beyond traditional roles

Another meaningful lesson from Lessons in Chemistry is that people should be allowed to define family and identity on their own terms.

Elizabeth's life challenges conventional ideas about motherhood, relationships, and women's responsibilities. Her experiences show that being a mother does not mean abandoning one's ambitions, just as pursuing a career does not make someone less capable of caring for a family.

The novel explores how people navigate grief, parenthood, relationships, and the expectations placed upon them. It presents a more nuanced understanding of what it means to build a fulfilling life.

Elizabeth refuses to accept that she must choose between being intellectually ambitious and being a devoted parent. Instead, she creates a life that reflects her circumstances, values, and priorities.

For readers, the lesson is that there is no single formula for a meaningful life. People have different ambitions, responsibilities, and definitions of happiness.

Rather than measuring ourselves against conventional milestones, we can focus on building lives that align with our own values and allow us to grow.

Final thoughts

Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus is more than a novel about a scientist navigating a world that underestimates her. It is a story about challenging inequality, embracing curiosity, and refusing to let other people's assumptions determine your future.

Through Elizabeth Zott's experiences, readers are reminded that intelligence deserves recognition, women deserve equal opportunities, and personal ambition should not be sacrificed to satisfy society's expectations.

The five lessons from the book encourage us to question outdated beliefs, trust our abilities, and create lives that reflect who we truly are. Whether you are navigating your career, questioning social norms, or discovering your own identity, Elizabeth's journey offers a powerful reminder that you do not have to fit into someone else's definition of success.

Ultimately, Lessons in Chemistry encourages readers to approach life with curiosity, courage, and the confidence to challenge what they have been told is possible.

item.title: 5 lessons to learn from Sorrow and Bliss by Meg Mason
item.description: Discover five powerful lessons from Sorrow and Bliss by Meg Mason about mental health, relationships, family, and finding happiness
item.content:encoded:
Sorrow and Bliss by Meg Mason is a moving novel about mental health, marriage, family relationships, and the complicated experience of living with emotional pain.

The story follows Martha Friel, a woman in her forties who struggles with an unnamed mental illness that affects her relationships, her sense of identity, and her ability to navigate everyday life.

Through Martha's experiences, Mason explores the challenges of understanding oneself when one's emotions feel difficult to explain. The novel also examines how mental health struggles can affect loved ones and how compassion, patience, and acceptance can help people navigate difficult periods in their lives.

Rather than offering simple answers, Sorrow and Bliss presents an honest portrayal of a woman trying to understand herself while learning to live with uncertainty.

5 Important lessons readers can learn from Meg Mason's novel

1. Mental health struggles are not always visible

One of the most significant lessons from Sorrow and Bliss is that emotional pain is not always easy to recognise from the outside.

Martha often struggles internally in ways that other people cannot fully understand. Her behaviour, relationships, and reactions are shaped by difficulties she cannot easily explain, making it challenging for those around her to understand what she is experiencing. The novel highlights how someone can appear functional in certain areas of life while privately struggling to cope.

It challenges the assumption that people who seem capable, articulate, or outwardly comfortable are necessarily doing well emotionally. This lesson reminds us to approach others with empathy rather than making assumptions about their lives. We rarely know the full story behind someone's behaviour, and a little patience can make a meaningful difference.

Mental health deserves the same compassion and understanding as any other aspect of a person's well-being.

2. Love does not always mean understanding someone completely

Relationships are central to Martha's story, particularly her marriage to Patrick. Their relationship illustrates how love can coexist with confusion, frustration, and emotional distance.

Sometimes, the people closest to us genuinely care about us but struggle to understand what we are going through. They may want to help without knowing what to say or how to respond. Sorrow and Bliss explores the difficult reality that loving someone does not automatically give us the ability to understand every part of their experience. Relationships can become complicated when emotional struggles affect communication, expectations, and everyday responsibilities.

The novel encourages readers to recognise that meaningful relationships require more than affection. They also need honesty, patience, communication, and a willingness to acknowledge what we do not understand.

Love may not solve every problem, but a willingness to listen and learn can help people feel less alone in their struggles.

3. You do not have to have everything figured out

Martha's journey is not a straightforward story of personal growth in which every problem eventually disappears. Instead, she navigates uncertainty, difficult emotions, and questions about who she is and what she wants from life.

Her experiences remind readers that personal growth rarely follows a perfect timeline. Some people understand themselves early in life, while others spend years trying to make sense of their emotions, relationships, and choices. There is no universal deadline for becoming confident, finding stability, or understanding what makes us happy. The pressure to have a successful career, a healthy relationship, and a clear sense of identity can make people feel as though they are falling behind. Martha's story challenges this expectation by showing how complicated real life can be.

The lesson is to permit yourself to be a work in progress. You can make mistakes, change your mind, and take time to understand yourself without treating uncertainty as a personal failure.

4. Family relationships can be complicated and imperfect

Family plays an important role in Sorrow and Bliss, particularly through Martha's relationships with her parents and sister, Ingrid.

The novel portrays family as a source of both comfort and conflict. Family members may care deeply about one another while still misunderstanding each other's needs, struggling to communicate, or carrying unresolved tensions. These relationships demonstrate that affection does not automatically remove differences or prevent people from hurting one another. Sometimes, family members have difficulty recognising experiences that are different from their own. Mason presents these dynamics with humour and emotional honesty, showing that family relationships are rarely as simple as they appear from the outside.

The lesson is that understanding within a family requires effort. Listening without judgement, recognising individual differences, and acknowledging past hurt can help create healthier relationships.

It is also important to remember that complicated family dynamics do not mean that every relationship is beyond repair. With willingness and appropriate boundaries, people can find new ways to relate to one another.

Also Read
5 Non-fiction books you must read before 2026 ends

5. Happiness does not mean living without sorrow

The title Sorrow and Bliss captures one of the novel's central ideas: life can contain happiness and pain at the same time.

Martha's experiences challenge the belief that a fulfilling life must be free from sadness, uncertainty, or emotional difficulty. Her journey is not simply about eliminating suffering but about understanding how her struggles fit into her larger experience of living.

People often postpone happiness until they believe everything is in order. They may think they can only feel content once their relationships improve, their careers become stable, or their emotional difficulties disappear. However, life rarely unfolds so neatly. The novel encourages readers to recognise that difficult emotions do not erase moments of connection, humour, love, or joy. A person can experience pain while still appreciating meaningful parts of life.

This does not mean ignoring suffering or pretending that everything is fine. Instead, it means allowing room for different emotions without believing that one difficult chapter defines an entire life.

Final thoughts

Sorrow and Bliss by Meg Mason is a deeply human novel about mental health, relationships, family, and the complicated process of understanding oneself. Through Martha Friel's experiences, it explores the realities of emotional suffering without reducing them to easy answers or simple solutions.

The five lessons from the novel remind us to approach mental health with empathy, recognise that love requires understanding, give ourselves time to grow, accept the imperfections of family relationships, and make space for both sorrow and happiness.

Ultimately, the book offers a compassionate reminder that people are more complicated than their struggles. Understanding ourselves and others may take time, but patience, honesty, and empathy can help us navigate the uncertainty of being human.

item.title: Microsoft announces voluntary exit offer for employees in India, 3 other countries
item.description: Microsoft has about 23,000 employees in India, although there is no immediate clarity on how many of them would be eligible for the voluntary exit programme.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft on Monday announced a voluntary exit programme for eligible employees in India, the US, the UK and Canada, offering financial support and career planning resources to those opting to leave the company, according to a blog post by the tech giant.

Microsoft has about 23,000 employees in India, although there is no immediate clarity on how many of them would be eligible for the voluntary exit programme. Globally, around 60,000 employees are eligible.

It is learnt that eligible employees in India will have until December 1 to decide on the voluntary exit offer.

The package is understood to be similar to a standard severance arrangement, including one month's base salary for each completed year of service, plus health insurance and career transition services.

Microsoft's Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer Amy Coleman informed in her blog post that the voluntary exit offer (VEO), which will be available to employees at level 70 and below (internal job grades that span various levels of seniority at Microsoft) in participating teams across the four countries, is a time-limited initiative aimed at providing greater flexibility to employees considering opportunities outside the company.

The offer will be available to eligible employees in participating teams in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States, she wrote in the post.

Meanwhile, a Microsoft spokesperson said the company continues to invest in India's talent and technology ecosystem and is backing the country's AI ambitions with $20.5 billion in committed investment between 2025 and 2029 across cloud and AI infrastructure, skilling and operations.

"We are also on track to fulfil our commitment of equipping 20 million people across India with AI skills by 2030," the Microsoft spokesperson said.

Coleman - in her blog post - said the programme would provide employees with an option to make the transition with support, while allowing participating businesses to adjust their workforce according to evolving requirements.

"This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organisations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs," Coleman said.

The company clarified that the programme would not be implemented uniformly across its operations, with participation depending on individual business priorities, customer commitments and workforce requirements.

Eligible employees will receive emails detailing the terms of their voluntary exit offers, the blog post said.

"The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We'll learn from it," Coleman said.

She added that Microsoft would continue helping employees develop new skills and explore internal career opportunities, where appropriate.

"There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee," Coleman said, emphasising that the company would seek to balance changing business requirements with opportunities for employees to grow and contribute.

item.title: Why women should build their front row; AI automation and its impact on jobs
item.description: Kripa Venkatachalam, VP, India Technical Field Organisation & Global Customer Success at Cadence Design Systems, reflects on gender barriers, changing workplace policies, and the importance of having people who cheer you.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

India’s ambition to achieve defence self-reliance gets a big boost. 

Sarvam has inked a five-year agreement with the defence ministry to develop AI tech for the armed forces. The Bengaluru-based AI company will design, develop and deploy AI applications for operations, training, and decision-support, and also provide follow-on technical assistance. The deal envisages shared foundation models, agentic infrastructure, and geospatial and perception systems.

In other news, the high-stakes boardroom battle at the Tata Group continues. 

Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata has challenged the resolution to reappoint N Chandrasekaran as the chairman of Tata Sons. The resolution was passed at the board meeting of the Tata conglomerate’s holding company on September 17.  

According to sources, Noel has called the reappointment “void”, arguing that it was taken out of turn and was not on the meeting’s agenda. 

Meanwhile, as it reshapes its workforce amid heavy AI investments, Microsoft is offering employees an exit option. 

The American tech major has announced a voluntary exit programme for eligible employees in India, the US, the UK, and Canada. The package includes one month’s base salary for each completed year of service, besides health insurance and career transition services. Globally, around 60,000 employees are eligible for the programme. Microsoft has about 23,000 employees in India. However, it’s not clear how many would be eligible in the country. 

Lastly, Wall Street is closely watching the upcoming Big Tech earnings, which could serve as testimony to AI growth in an otherwise turbulent market. 

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • Why women should build their front row
  • AI automation and its impact on jobs

Women in Tech

Kripa Venkatachalam of Cadence urges women to build their front row

As part of our Women in Tech series, Kripa Venkatachalam, VP, India Technical Field Organisation & Global Customer Success at Cadence Design Systems, reflects on gender barriers, changing workplace policies, mentorship, and the importance of having people who egg you on.

Her career spanning more than two decades has taken her through diverse roles across companies, including LSI Logic Corporation, Synopsys, GlobalFoundries, and Siemens EDA. Today, as VP, India Technical Field Organisation & Global Customer Success at Cadence Design Systems, she has what she calls a “front-row seat” to how the world’s chips are designed in India.

Key takeaways: 

  • Kripa believes women need to seek support, leverage their network, and not always put the burden on themselves. “You have to make your family work for you, your workplace work for you, your society work for you. You have to lean in and take the help,” she says.
  • At informal forums in Cadence, she often speaks about the need for people, especially women, to create their own front row—people cheering for them. “The front row has to assure you. Organisations and managers have to look closer, look harder, and encourage women forward,” she reiterates. 
  • As she looks ahead, Kripa resists the idea of tying her ambitions to a title. She describes her career as a jungle gym rather than a ladder, an image she credits to Sheryl Sandberg.

Capital no longer creates jobs: Yatish Rajawat of Hundred Million Jobs

At TechSparks 2026, K Yatish Rajawat, Co-founder of Hundred Million Jobs, a non-profit initiative to create 100 million net jobs in India over the next decade, said MSMEs, data laws, entrepreneurship and reskilling will shape the next wave of employment in the country.

Key takeaways: 

  • Rajawat identified three trends reshaping the economy. One, the old formula, wherein Rs 100 crore of investment generates around 10,000 jobs, no longer holds, said Rajawat. Schemes such as the production-linked incentive are tied to capital rather than employment, he added. 
  • The second trend is the impact of AI and automation. AI is already affecting white-collar work across sectors. MSMEs, which he called the country’s largest job engine, are also losing jobs to automation.
  • The third is platform consolidation. Rajawat argued that dominant ecommerce and social media platforms hold consumer data, which new entrepreneurs need, and this kind of monopoly prevents new businesses from succeeding. If entrepreneurship stalls, so does job creation, he said.

item.title: Nazara Technologies swings to profit in Q2; revenue jumps 53% to Rs 803 Cr
item.description: Nazara Technologies swung to a profit of Rs 35.3 crore in Q2 FY27, as revenue surged 53% year-on-year to a record Rs 803 crore. Gaming revenue more than doubled, driven by growth in mobile gaming and the consolidation of Bluetile and BestPlay.
item.content:encoded:
Nazara Technologies on Monday reported a profit after tax of about Rs 35.3 crore for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, against a loss of about Rs 34 crore in the year-ago period, as the gaming company clinched a "record quarter" in revenue.

For the second quarter of FY2026-27, the revenue rose 53% year-on-year to a record Rs 803 crore.

The EBITDA - earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, a measure of a company's operating profitability - grew 93% to Rs 120 crore, with the margin expanding 311 basis points to 14.9%.

Profit after tax from continuing operations was Rs 35 crore, compared with a loss of Rs 34 crore in Q2FY26.

Q2 FY27 is the first quarter to include Bluetile and BestPlay, consolidated from August 1. In their first two months, the two businesses generated revenue of Rs 329 crore, up 49%, and EBITDA of Rs 64 crore, up 64%, at a margin of 19.4% against 17.5%.

Gaming revenue grew 122% to Rs 656 crore at a 21.5% EBITDA margin, accounting for 82% of consolidated revenue.

Mobile gaming revenue jumped 167% to Rs 550 crore.

Among existing studios, WildWorks grew revenue 41%, Kiddopia 21% and Curve Games 27%, with Curve's EBITDA rising 61%.

"This quarter demonstrates the company we are building: a portfolio of high-quality games on a single, shared platform," Raymond A. Stauffer, CEO, Nazara Technologies, said.

He added: "Every game we launch and every studio we acquire benefits from proven capabilities from the outset, enabling us to scale faster and more profitably."

Stauffer, founder of Bluetile and BestPlay, became CEO on September 16. Mithun Sacheti, founder of CaratLane, joined as Executive Director on October 12, subject to shareholder approval, and Arun Agarwal joined as Chief Financial Officer on October 16.

Together, the team brings global gaming, operating and financial depth to scale Nazara's platform, the release said.

item.title: Noel Tata challenges resolution to reappoint Chandrasekaran as Tata Sons chairman
item.description: Noel Tata wrote to Tata Sons' company secretary Suprakash Mukhopadhyay on Monday, challenging the resolution for the reappointment of Chandrasekaran beyond February 2027 as well, which brought the ruptures inside the over-century-old conglomerate's board out in the open.
item.content:encoded:
Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata on Monday challenged the resolution to reappoint N Chandrasekaran as the chairman of Tata Sons, which was passed at the September 17 board meeting of the holding company of the country's largest conglomerate.

Noel Tata wrote to Tata Sons' company secretary Suprakash Mukhopadhyay on Monday, challenging the resolution for the reappointment of Chandrasekaran beyond February 2027 as well, which brought the ruptures inside the over-century-old conglomerate's board out in the open.

Sources privy to the development said Noel has termed the reappointment for five years as void, basing his argument on a slew of factors, including notice and the agenda for the meeting.

Noel contended that the reappointment was taken out of turn and it was not on the agenda at all for the meeting, the sources said, adding that it was limited to a debriefing from the nomination and remuneration committee.

Emails sent to Tata Sons and Tata Trusts seeking comments on the matter did not elicit an immediate response.

Noel, who heads the Tata Trusts that own two-thirds of Tata Sons, had opposed Chandrasekaran's reappointment when it had been put to vote. Venu Srinivasan, the second of the Tata Trusts' directors on the board of Tata Sons, sided with the majority in favour of the reappointment.

Other directors who had voted in favour of Chandrasekaran's reappointment at the meeting included Anita George, Harish Manwani, and Saurabh Agarwal.

As per Tata Sons' Articles of Association, Tata Trusts' nominee directors have to give their affirmative vote for a resolution to be passed, Noel contended.

In the letter, Noel also sought an unedited video recording of the board meeting, according to the sources.

item.title: Anthropic files for IPO even as losses surge to $80B
item.description: Anthropic will be listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange and will trade under the name of ANT.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic, one of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) companies and the developer of the large language model Claude, has filed for an initial public offering (IPO), moving closer to becoming a publicly listed company.

The company plans to list on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.

Anthropic was co-founded by Dario Amodei and others in 2021. In the first half of 2026, it reported revenue of $16.2 billion, while losses stood at $80.74 billion. In comparison, the company reported revenue of $1.16 billion and losses of $12.96 billion in the first half of 2025.

Anthropic’s growth has been remarkable, with revenue rising from just $41 million in 2023 to $4.5 billion in 2025.

However, the company has not specified a date for its Nasdaq listing, disclosed the proposed share price or stated how much it plans to raise through the IPO.

Anthropic’s IPO is expected to be closely watched across the technology industry, given the rapid advances made by AI companies. The company was valued at $965 billion in its most recent funding round in May 2026.

Interestingly, Anthropic market rival OpenAI has said it will go for a public listing next year.

In its IPO filing, Anthropic said, “We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach and solve problems that have resisted generations of human efforts.”

“Anthropic aims to realise these while navigating and preventing the risks that come with a technological revolution this fast and this powerful.”

Anthropic believes the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning. It further noted that the world has only begun to use the capabilities of today’s frontier models, and the gap between what Claude can do and how broadly it is used represents one of our largest growth opportunities, alongside continued advances at the frontier.

item.title: Healthtech startup Cent raises $15M in Series A
item.description: Cent said it will use the funding for R&D and to build out its AI, engineering, and clinical teams.
item.content:encoded:
Healthtech startup Cent has raised $15 million in a Series A funding round through a combination of debt and equity, led by Blume Ventures and existing investor South Park Commons.

The round also saw participation from individual investors, including Arun Sarin, former CEO of Vodafone; Srinivas Narayanan, former CTO (B2B) of OpenAI; and Sharath Narayana, Krishna Sridhar, and Aprameya Radhakrishna.

Cent said it will use the funding for R&D and to build out its AI, engineering, and clinical teams.

Cent was founded by Shashank ND, Arpit Garg, and Anshul Khandelwal in 2025 and is positioned as a preventive health intelligence company. Shashank ND is the founder of Practo, while Anshul Khandelwal was the former CMO of Ola Electric, and Arpit Garg was the former product head at Lenskart.

Cent is building a vertically integrated preventive health platform that combines purpose-built hardware, AI-driven radiology and diagnostics, and bioinformatics. The startup says the platform can help detect diseases well before symptoms appear.

Cent has also acquired Medsee, an AI-powered radiology reporting workflow platform founded by Chitra Singh and designed for qualified medical professionals. The platform drafts structured reports and highlights findings for radiologist review, enabling Cent to deliver faster, more consistent reporting as scan volumes grow.

"India's healthcare system is still built to treat illness, not to find it early. We believe the next shift is preventive care that is precise and accessible at scale. This investment lets us go deeper into AI, medical imaging and clinical research, and build preventive health infrastructure in India that can serve the world," said Anshul Khandelwal, Co-Founder, Cent.

According to Cent, it has completed 10,000 preventive whole-body scans across Bengaluru, Mumbai and Delhi since inception. It is targeting 10 million scans by 2035.

“We are believers in the Cent's vision to extend this from India to the world over time, and it is in line with our conviction around health tech for a decade now," said Karthik Reddy, Co-founder and Managing Partner, Blume Ventures.

item.title: Google Cloud’s Gemini voice AI wants to do more than just talk
item.description: What if AI could do more than answer the phone? At TechSparks 2026, Google Cloud’s Naren Kachroo showed Gemini voice AI handling bookings, sales negotiations and multilingual conversations.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine asking an AI assistant to find a customer, negotiate a price and help close a sale, all without typing a single prompt. Voice AI is moving beyond answering questions to taking on tasks, and Google Cloud wants businesses to put it to work.

At TechSparks 2026, Naren Kachroo, Head of AI Go-to-Market at Google Cloud, demonstrated how Gemini’s voice AI capabilities could help businesses handle customer conversations, restaurant bookings and sales negotiations.

From talking to taking action

Until now, much of the AI experience has revolved around asking questions and getting answers. Kachroo said the next step is AI that can access information, use tools and take action on a user’s behalf.

“We don't want to focus on voice AI just being an experience to talk to AI,” he said. “We want voice AI to be powered through agentic experiences where the task is actually accomplished with AI.”

To show what that means, Naren Kachroo played a demonstration of an AI assistant booking a restaurant table for eight. The assistant answered questions about bringing a birthday cake, identified a dish from an image, discussed vegetarian options and switched between English and Spanish during the conversation.

In other words, it did more than take a booking. It handled the questions that came with it, too.

Kachroo also introduced Gemini Live voice capabilities, alongside models for text-to-speech, speech-to-text and translation. He showcased Live Avatar, which combines voice interaction with a visual AI presence.

Meet the AI sales assistant

The standout demonstration involved a fictional safety equipment business with 500 helmets sitting in its inventory. Its owner, Rajesh, wanted to sell them quickly and instructed an AI voice agent to find a suitable lead, contact the customer and negotiate a price above Rs 400 per helmet.

The assistant checked the business’s leads, identified a construction company that needed 500 helmets and initiated a call in Hindi. When the prospective buyer pushed for a lower price, the AI negotiated while sticking to the owner’s pricing instruction.

It was a glimpse of how AI could help small businesses manage sales without handling every step themselves. The agent could draw on internal business information, speak to a customer and respond to objections, rather than simply recommend what the owner should do next.

Kachroo said the demonstration showed how the agent maintained context as it moved from internal information to a customer conversation.

Why India needs voice AI

Voice could be particularly useful in India, where people speak many languages and have different levels of comfort with typing or navigating digital interfaces.

“I believe that India and Indian consumer is continuing to go as voice first,” Naren said.

He highlighted Google’s work on Indian languages, accents and cultural nuances, and pointed to Equal AI, an Indian company building voice assistants that can handle calls on users’ behalf.

For Kachroo, the goal is to make voice AI useful in everyday business processes, not just impressive in a demo. That means building systems that understand context, handle interruptions and follow instructions while completing tasks.

The real test, then, is not whether AI can hold a conversation. It is whether it can get the job done. And for businesses exploring voice AI, that could be the difference between another chatbot and a genuinely useful assistant.

item.title: Ather turns profitable after Rs 154 Cr loss; Meta plans to raise $35B for AI expansion
item.description: Ather Energy swung to a consolidated net profit in Q2 FY27 as revenue from operations grew 63% year-on-year. The electric two-wheeler maker plans to expand production capacity to meet rising demand.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader, 

MakeMyTrip is back in the black! The travel booking platform reported a net profit of $1.8 million in Q2 FY27, compared with a $5.7 million loss a year ago. Revenue rose 2.5% year-on-year to $235.2 million, or 11.2% in constant-currency terms, driven by increased bookings across categories.

Meanwhile, Anthropic, one of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) companies and the developer of the large language model Claude, has filed for an initial public offering (IPO), moving closer to becoming a publicly listed company. The company plans to list on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.

In other news, healthtech startup BioStack has raised $9.5 million in seed funding, led by Peak XV, with participation from Afore Capital, DCVC and other investors. The startup integrates fragmented clinical records to support healthcare research and clinical decision-making. It plans to use the funds to expand internationally, strengthen its technology and grow its engineering and research teams.

The AI infrastructure boom continues to gather pace. Tata Communications plans to invest $450 million to build a high-speed fibre network connecting AI data centres, catering to rising demand for AI and cloud computing infrastructure. The investment will expand its network capacity and enable faster, more reliable data transfer between data centres, which is critical for large-scale AI workloads. The move comes as technology companies ramp up investments in AI infrastructure, increasing the need for high-capacity connectivity alongside computing power. 

In a similar push to support AI expansion, Meta Platforms has launched stock and convertible preferred-stock offerings worth about $35 billion to fund its expanding AI infrastructure, including data centres and computing capacity. The Facebook and Instagram parent also plans a separate share-sale programme of up to $60 billion in 2027, potentially taking its planned equity fundraising to $95 billion.

Ather Energy swings to Rs 1.26 Cr profit in Q2

Electric two-wheeler maker Ather Energy reported a consolidated net profit of Rs 1.26 crore in Q2 FY27, compared with a net loss of Rs 154 crore in the year-ago quarter. The company’s total income rose 62% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs 1,527 crore, supported by growth in vehicle sales and operations. Ather’s performance reflects improving scale and operational efficiency as it works towards sustained profitability.

Key takeaways: 

  • Ather Energy reported a net profit of Rs 1.26 crore in Q2 FY27, compared with a loss of Rs 154 crore a year earlier. 
  • The company’s total income increased 62% YoY to Rs 1,527 crore during the quarter.

TechSparks

QpiAI founder Nagendra Nagaraja makes the case for intelligence modelling 

Nagendra Nagaraja, founder, CEO and chairman of QpiAI, believes the future of artificial intelligence lies beyond language models and conventional computing. Speaking at TechSparks 2026, he advocated for “intelligence modelling” to discover new knowledge rather than simply automate tasks. He argued that quantum computing could help overcome the limitations of silicon chips and large language models by processing complex data found in nature.

Key takeaways: 

  • Nagaraja said conventional AI relies heavily on digitised human knowledge and argued that intelligence modelling should focus on discovering what is not yet known. 
  • He highlighted quantum computing’s potential to solve complex problems in areas such as agriculture, materials science, and financial fraud detection.
